summary: Describes how a CBOR Web Token (CWT) can state that the presenter holds a particular proof-of-possession key, so holding the token alone is not enough. It provides the CBOR equivalent of the JWT feature in RFC 7800.

eli5.summary: A ticket that also says you must show a special matching key to use it. Then a stranger who finds the ticket cannot use it.

subtitle: How a CBOR Web Token says that whoever presents it must also prove they hold a particular key.

tldr.problem: A plain token can be used by anyone who gets hold of it. An issuer needs a way to bind a CWT to a key that only the legitimate presenter holds.
tldr.mechanism: The CWT carries a cnf (confirmation) claim, claim key 8, whose CBOR map holds the key (COSE_Key, key 1), an encrypted key (Encrypted_COSE_Key, key 2) or a key identifier (kid, key 3).
tldr.outcome: A recipient can cryptographically confirm that the presenter holds the key. It is the CBOR counterpart of RFC 7800 for JWTs and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8747 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2020, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the CBOR equivalent of RFC 7800.

sections.title: Proof of Possession for CWTs
sections.content:
RFC 8747 describes how a CBOR Web Token (CWT, RFC 8392) can declare that the presenter of the token possesses a particular proof-of-possession (PoP) key. This is sometimes called holder-of-key. It gives the same functionality as RFC 7800 does for JSON Web Tokens, but using CBOR instead of JSON.

The RFC defines three roles. The issuer creates the CWT and binds the claims about the subject to the PoP key. The presenter proves possession of a private or secret key to a recipient. The recipient receives the CWT. In OAuth terms, the presenter is the client and the recipient is the resource server.
sections.eli5: A normal ticket works for whoever holds it. This kind of ticket also names a secret key, so only the person with that key can use it.

sections.title: The cnf Confirmation Claim
sections.content:
By including a cnf (confirmation) claim, the issuer declares that the presenter possesses a particular key and that the recipient can cryptographically confirm it. The claim value is a CBOR map whose members identify the key.

The presenter can be identified by the CWT in several ways. Some applications use the sub claim, others the iss claim, and the choice depends on the application.

The set of confirmation members a valid CWT must contain is context dependent and outside the scope of the RFC. Absent other requirements, confirmation members that an implementation does not understand MUST be ignored. A cnf claim MUST represent only a single PoP key, and at most one of COSE_Key and Encrypted_COSE_Key may be present. An application that needs several keys can use other claim names with the same syntax.
sections.eli5: The ticket has a little box labelled cnf. Inside is either the key, a locked copy of it, or just a label saying which key to use.

sections.title: Three Ways to Carry the Key
sections.content:
Asymmetric key. The COSE_Key member (key 1) holds a COSE_Key for the public key matching the presenter's private key. It MUST contain the required members for its key type and MAY contain others, including kid. It MAY also hold a symmetric key if the CWT itself is encrypted; if the CWT is not encrypted, a symmetric key MUST be encrypted as described next.

Encrypted symmetric key. The Encrypted_COSE_Key member (key 2) holds a COSE_Key for the symmetric key, encrypted to a key known to the recipient using COSE_Encrypt or COSE_Encrypt0. The plaintext is the COSE_Key representation.

Key ID. The kid member (key 3) is a binary string that identifies the key instead of carrying it, provided the recipient can obtain the key from the ID. Its content is application specific; an application may, for example, use a cryptographic hash of the public key.

If a Key ID is not derived cryptographically from the key, or not all parties validate that derivation, expect collisions where different keys get the same ID. Recipients should be prepared to handle that.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to name the key: put it right in the ticket, put in a locked copy that only the checker can open, or write down a nickname the checker already knows.

sections.title: What the RFC Leaves Unspecified
sections.content:
Proof of possession is often shown by having the presenter sign a value chosen by the recipient, called a nonce or a challenge. Other means of showing freshness exist, such as those used in authentication and key exchange protocols.

The RFC intentionally does not say how the nonce is communicated, what it contains, or how the signed nonce is sent back, because that differs between protocols. Applications that use other proof methods are encouraged to register them in the CWT Confirmation Methods registry.
sections.eli5: The ticket says a key is needed, but it does not say how the checker tests you. That part is left to whatever system uses the ticket.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
All security considerations of RFC 8392 apply. Possessing a key is only valuable if it is kept secret. Applications using proof of possession SHOULD also use audience restriction so recipients can reject messages meant for others.

The proof only gives the intended gain when it is current and not replayed, so protocols can use nonces and timestamps. The CWT needs data origin authentication and integrity protection, by a keyed message digest or digital signature. A symmetric key inside a CWT also needs confidentiality protection. Proof-of-possession signatures made with keys that do not meet the application's trust criteria MUST NOT be relied upon.

For privacy, a PoP key can act as a correlation handle if it is reused, so different PoP keys should be used with different parties.
sections.eli5: A key only helps if it stays secret, and the check must be fresh so nobody can replay an old answer. Using the same key everywhere also lets people track you.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The parties must share extra information: the recipient needs credentials to verify the CWT and may need to decrypt it, and issuer and recipient must agree on the claims used.

An issuer that puts a Key ID in a CWT must not issue another CWT with different claims and the same Key ID within the CWTs' lifetime, unless that is intended. Otherwise one party could impersonate another. A deliberate case is when a presenter gets a CWT with extended scope for the same recipient and wants to keep an existing security association such as a DTLS session. If PoP keys serve several kinds of CWTs, keep the keys for each kind segregated; audience restriction is one mitigation.
sections.eli5: Do not hand out the same nickname for two different keys while tickets are still valid, or someone could pretend to be someone else.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the cnf claim with claim key 8 and value type map in the CWT Claims registry. It also creates the CWT Confirmation Methods registry for cnf members, with Specification Required registration after a three-week review period on a mailing list and advice from designated experts.

The initial contents are COSE_Key (1, JWT name jwk), Encrypted_COSE_Key (2, JWT name jwe) and kid (3, JWT name kid).
sections.eli5: The names and numbers for the three boxes were written in an official list, and new boxes can be added later after review.
